item.title: The case for a personal changelog
item.description:
Every repo I own keeps a CHANGELOG.md, and beyond that there is one plain text file with the things that do not belong to a repo: a firewall rule, a DNS entry, a systemd unit that exists for a reason I will not remember.

The format is deliberately boring — date, what changed, why, and how to undo it. Ten seconds per entry, and it has already answered “why is this port open” twice this year.

item.title: Email forwarding with Cloudflare: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC
item.description:
A forwarder doesn’t rewrite anything, so authentication breaks by design: Cloudflare isn’t in the sender’s SPF, and the forwarding hop modifies the body, so DKIM fails too. Gmail sees exactly that and warns. The fix is honest DNS, not a better product.

MX points at mx.cloudflare.net; SPF authorizes Cloudflare’s include alongside whatever sends your mail; DMARC starts relaxed (p=none; aspf=r; adkim=r) so forwarded mail isn’t punished, then tightens once deliverability is stable. DKIM can’t survive the forwarded path — Cloudflare doesn’t sign — but it’s still worth setting up for outbound mail sent through Gmail, so your own messages align.

item.title: Ext4 superblock repair and file recovery
item.description:
Can't read superblock means the OS can’t find the filesystem’s own index. The sequence that avoids making things worse: lsblk -f and blkid to confirm you’re mounting the partition, not the disk; file -s to see what’s actually there — crypto_LUKS or an LVM member needs unlocking before any fsck. Only then, unmounted, fsck.ext4 -f.

If the primary superblock is dead, ext filesystems keep backups. mke2fs -n lists their locations; fsck.ext4 -b 32768 repairs from one. When fsck reports a zero-length partition and dmesg shows medium errors, stop and image with ddrescue — the repair happens on the copy, never the patient.

item.title: HTTP files: runnable API requests in the repository
item.description:
An .http file is plain text: requests separated by ###, runnable from VS Code’s REST Client or the JetBrains HTTP client, importable into Postman and Insomnia. The format’s only real feature is that it lives next to the code in the repository.

That changes behavior. Example calls get updated in the same PR as the endpoint, environments are files (*.http.env.json for VS Code, http-client.env.json for JetBrains) with {{baseUrl}} and {{token}} variables, and pre-request scripts handle login and token chaining. New teammates learn the API by running five lines instead of reading a wiki that’s been stale since the auth rewrite.

item.title: Immutable Linux: OSTree, rpm-ostree, and Arch trade-offs
item.description:
OSTree versions an entire OS filesystem: commits, read-only root, instant rollback — “git for /usr”, with no opinion about packages. rpm-ostree builds on it and adds what Silverblue and Kinoite actually run: atomic upgrades, layered packages, rollback that is one reboot away.

Arch has neither. The honest options are (a) an Arch-based immutable distro (Aurora, Bluefin, blendOS), or (b) DIY with Btrfs snapshots, a read-only root, and Distrobox for apps. Option (b) gives rollback, not immutability: root can remount rw, and pacman updates aren’t transactional. Building OSTree on Arch by hand is a hobby project with poor documentation.

item.title: Maildir, IMAP, and webmail frontends
item.description:
Maildir’s advantage is that it isn’t interesting: one file per message across cur, new, tmp. You can grep it, rsync it, back it up with any tool that copies files, and switch clients without exporting anything. Every proprietary mailbox format has spent years failing to be worth as much.

The access paths: Dovecot for personal and small-server IMAP — simple, modular, Maildir-native; Cyrus only when scale and ACLs demand it. In front, Roundcube or SnappyMail if you want a browser client; Mailpile or Piler when the actual goal is browsing and searching old mail without running a mail server at all.

item.title: Mapperly: multi-source mapping, fallback, and records
item.description:
Mapperly’s pitch is compile-time mapping with no reflection. Multi-source works: pass two parameters, matching names and types combine, mismatches resolve via MapProperty or a custom method. Records work too, mapped through their constructor.

The gap is conditional fallback. There’s no “primary ?? fallback” concept, so you write a custom mapping method whose signature matches the source properties — and when name matching gets picky, add explicit MapProperty per field. For records, the clean shape is a Merge extension that builds the immutable result field by field; reflection-based generic merges break required constructor parameters and immutability, which is exactly what records are for.

item.title: MediaTek MT7921e Wi-Fi troubleshooting on Linux
item.description:
lspci -k names the driver; dmesg | grep mt7921e names the failure. For the MediaTek MT7921e the bar is low: driver own failed, DEAUTH_LEAVING, cards that don’t come back after suspend.

The workarounds, in the order I’d try them: update kernel and linux-firmware first, because regressions arrive with rolling releases and vanish the same way. Disable power saving (wifi.powersave = 2 for NetworkManager). If resume is the problem, a sleep hook reloads the module. For high-throughput streaming, MTU 1400 stops Steam Link from drowning the card, and pcie_aspm=off is the last resort for PCIe power-saving crashes.

item.title: Task.WhenAll: exception handling and cancellation
item.description:
A try/catch around await Task.WhenAll(...) sees one exception. If four calls failed, the logs show one and the rest vanish into the task. Task.WhenAll throws the first one while still collecting every fault on its Exception property — which is an AggregateException you have to ask for.

So keep the task in a variable, catch, then walk whenAll.Exception?.InnerExceptions to log all of them. Cancellation is a separate channel: OperationCanceledException never appears in that aggregate, because cancellation is cooperative behavior, not a fault. Check TaskStatus when you need to tell “cancelled” from “failed.”

item.title: Riding OneDrive on Linux (it still hurts)
item.description:
There is no first-party client, so the realistic options are a browser or the abraunegg client. The client wins on the one thing that matters: it can be trusted to run headless as a systemd user service.

First run goes out with --dry-run and a conflict policy I chose on purpose (--resync is the sledgehammer; read what it deletes before running it). Inotify watches on a large tree need fs.inotify.max_user_watches raised, and the sync log is the actual interface — read it or be surprised.

item.title: Context switching: costs and mitigation practices
item.description:
Technical work runs on a loaded mental model — code paths, business rules, failure modes. Every interruption unloads it, and reloading isn’t instant. The numbers are stark: application switches cost up to 40% of productive time, recovery from a distraction averages 23 minutes, and interruptions arrive every 11. Most developers never reach full concentration, they just bounce between half-loaded states and call it productivity.

The AI twist makes it worse before better: more code generated means more PR contexts per developer, and review time and incidents rise with it. The job quietly shifts from creator to verifier, and verification isn’t free.

item.title: Copy-on-write in Linux: fork, shared memory, and IPC costs
item.description:
Isolation between processes is not a physical wall; it’s a per-process page table. Once you see memory that way, three things stop being magic.

fork copies the page table, not the memory: pages are shared and marked read-only, and the first write traps into the kernel, which copies that single 4 KB page. That’s why Redis can fork a 50 GB dataset to snapshot it while barely growing, and why write-heavy forks spike memory instead of failing upfront.

item.title: Turbo Pascal: fast compiles and the integrated toolchain
item.description:
Turbo Pascal’s innovation wasn’t the language — Pascal already existed. It was the loop: editor, compiler, and linker in one environment, compiling in seconds on hardware where other compilers took minutes, all on a floppy, priced for hobbyists. Units added separately compiled modules, and the dialect grew enough extensions to become its own standard.

Turbo C repeated the trick for C, and the echo is still audible: watch-recompile-run tooling, single-binary languages, and the general expectation that the edit-build-test cycle should be measured in seconds. The compiler that sells a workflow beats the compiler with better semantics — a lesson the JavaScript ecosystem relearns every few years.

item.title: Testcontainers with rootless Podman
item.description:
I run Podman rootless, which means the Docker socket Testcontainers expects simply is not there. The fix is one environment pair and a socket path that actually exists:

1
2

export DOCKER_HOST=unix:///run/user/$(id -u)/podman/podman.sock
export TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED=true

Ryuk needs a socket it can mount, and the rootless one is not it. Without Ryuk you own cleanup — a nightly podman ps --filter label=... sweep handles leftovers.

Two gotchas survived consolidation. The socket must be running (systemctl --user enable --now podman.socket), and Docker.DotNet caches the endpoint per process — set the variables before the first client is constructed, not inside a fixture.

item.title: Renovate, but for your compose files
item.description:
The mental model that unlocked Renovate for me: it is a match-and-replace engine, and the package ecosystems are just presets. A customManagers regex entry makes any version string in any file a dependency.

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8

{
 "customManagers": [{
 "customType": "regex",
 "fileMatch": ["docker-compose\\.ya?ml$"],
 "matchStrings": ["image: (?<depName>\\S+):(?<currentValue>\\S+)"],
 "datasourceTemplate": "docker"
 }]
}

The value is not freshness for its own sake — it is that the bump arrives as a pull request on a quiet morning instead of as a surprise during an incident. Digest pinning plus grouping keeps the noise proportional to the risk.

item.title: Blazor JS interop without the ceremony
item.description:
The interop that bites is the one called too early. During prerender there is no JavaScript, so anything in OnInitializedAsync that touches IJSRuntime either throws or silently no-ops depending on the render mode.

The shape that has held up: import the module once, keep the IJSObjectReference, call it in OnAfterRenderAsync(firstRender: true), and release it in IAsyncDisposable.

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8

private IJSObjectReference? module;

protected override async Task OnAfterRenderAsync(bool firstRender)
{
 if (!firstRender) return;
 module = await JS.InvokeAsync<IJSObjectReference>("import", "./chart.js");
 await module.InvokeVoidAsync("draw", elementRef);
}

One import per component instance is fine at this scale; the ceremony people add around shared module caching is a different problem.

item.title: Moving Forgejo from SQLite to PostgreSQL
item.description:
The symptom was a single file lock: first push after an idle night took about ten seconds, and CI plus webhooks stacked behind it. SQLite is a fine default right up to the moment several writers arrive.

The migration that worked: add a Postgres service to the compose file and point Forgejo at it via env; run forgejo dump for a full backup; extract gitea.db; then clean the SQLite copy for pgloader — drop columns that don’t exist in the Postgres schema and fix NULLs, which is the fiddly part. Start Forgejo against the empty Postgres so it creates the schema, import, verify users, tokens, hooks, and runners.

item.title: systemd timers without the ceremony
item.description:
Cron keeps getting replaced by two files that do what cron does plus logs, dependencies, and catch-up runs. The minimum pair:

1
2
3
4

# backup.timer
[Timer]
OnCalendar=daily
Persistent=true

with a Type=oneshot service beside it. Persistent=true is the one directive cron cannot give you: a missed run catches up after boot instead of silently skipping.

systemctl list-timers is the whole dashboard, and journalctl -u backup.service is the whole log story. RandomizedDelaySec on anything that phones home avoids the thundering herd at midnight.

item.title: Pull requests as reading practice
item.description:
I read pull requests I am not assigned to. Not to comment on every one — the habit is reading, and leaving a question only where a question is genuinely owed.

Fifteen minutes a day buys context that status meetings cannot: where the codebase is actually moving, which abstractions are straining, and who is about to need help.

The failure mode is turning reading into reviewing. Unrequested nitpicks cost the team more than the missed typo ever would; the rule I keep is that the comment must be worth the author’s next ten minutes.

item.title: Flaky tests are a scheduling problem
item.description:
Chasing a flaky test as a mystery wastes days. Chasing it as a scheduling bug is usually one afternoon, because the suspects are three: shared state between tests, dependence on wall-clock time, and dependence on real IO order.

The fixes are correspondingly boring. Fixtures that cannot leak (async setup/teardown per test, no static caches), a fake clock injected rather than DateTime.Now, and a container per suite instead of a shared database with yesterday’s rows.

item.title: Spec-driven development: intent, specs, and prompts
item.description:
The failure modes of vibe coding are consistent enough to name: collateral damage (fix one thing, break five), context amnesia (the agent undoes yesterday’s instruction to satisfy today’s), version blur (APIs invented from a training cutoff), and preferences that die with the session.

Spec-driven development answers with a long-lived markdown spec as the source of truth: intent lives in text, implementation can be regenerated, and the diff you review first is the spec, not the code. Spec-assisted is the lighter version — usage specs for third-party libraries so the agent works from current reality instead of memory.

item.title: Espresso: preinfusion by feel
item.description:
Wetting the puck at low flow for three to five seconds before opening the pump costs nothing and forgives a lot: fewer channeling spurts, and the first drops arrive sweeter instead of sharp.

It is not pressure profiling — it is one gesture, done by hand, at the lever. On my machine that is easing the pump on and counting. The puck saturates more evenly, so I can grind a notch finer and still hit the same time.

item.title: Recovering Lost Changes with JetBrains Rider Local History
item.description: Local History is one of those IDE features you don't think about until you desperately need it. This post covers what it is, how it works, and the scenarios where it saves you: accidental rollbacks, lost uncommitted changes and rebase mistakes.

item.title: DuckDB: SQL over CSV and Parquet files
item.description:
The moment a question spans three exported files, the options used to be Excel suffering or loading a warehouse. DuckDB is the third: an embedded columnar database that runs inside your process. Columnar storage means AVG(age) reads one column, not every row, and vectorized execution processes chunks of rows instead of one at a time.

Practically, it queries files directly — SELECT * FROM 'sales.csv', FROM read_parquet('data/*.parquet') — with no import step, and Parquet is where it shines because only the needed columns get read. It also works as a local ETL engine (CREATE TABLE clean AS SELECT ...) and as a Python data-science companion.

item.title: Process substitution in bash: <() and >() patterns
item.description:
Pipes need a program to read stdin. Process substitution doesn’t ask: <(cmd) presents command output as a file path, >(cmd) presents a writable path. The shell does it with a temporary entry in /proc, and cleanup is automatic.

The uses I keep: diff original.txt <(sed 's/old/new/g' original.txt) previews a transformation before sed -i commits it; diff <(sort a) <(sort b) compares content ignoring order; vim <(curl -s https://example.com/file) opens a remote file without saving it. The trick I know but rarely reach for: tar -czf - ./project | tee >(ssh box1 "tar -xzf - -C /dest") >(ssh box2 "tar -xzf - -C /dest") > /dev/null ships one archive to two servers concurrently.

item.title: Dockerfile practices: users, sudo, multi-stage, and layer order
item.description:
Two habits cover most of what a Dockerfile should be.

Security: root inside the container is root on the host kernel if anything escapes, so create a dedicated user and USER it. The common snag is ports below 1024 — either grant NET_BIND_SERVICE or listen on 8080 and let a proxy own the privilege. Don’t install sudo; it’s a setuid binary and a privilege-escalation path for an attacker who already has code execution. Multi-stage builds keep compilers and build tooling out of the runtime layer entirely.

item.title: Git recovery: reset modes, reflog, and bisect
item.description:
Git stops being scary once it’s pointers and snapshots instead of incantations. Working directory, index, repository — the state a change lives in decides which tool moves it back. Sketching current state versus desired state on paper is faster than guessing at commands.

That framing makes reset predictable: --soft moves only the branch pointer (fix the last commit), --mixed also resets the index (unstage and re-cut), --hard overwrites the working tree (you meant it, right). On pushed history, revert — reset plus force-push creates confusion for everyone else and an audit trail for nobody.

item.title: .NET memory: ArrayPool, Span, and stack allocation
item.description:
Pooling is a performance technique, not a virtue. HTTP connection pooling is essential; pooling small objects usually costs more than the GC it avoids. ArrayPool is the exception worth knowing because arrays are large, frequent, and awkward to allocate in hot loops.

The real implementation is instructive even if you never type it: power-of-two buckets (so a rental is at most 2x what you need), trimming under memory pressure, per-core lists to reduce contention, and a thread-static cache in front of the shared queues. The pattern that pays: stackalloc into a Span for short buffers, rent from the pool for large ones, return in finally.

item.title: Btrfs snapshots before you need them
item.description:
Hourly snapshots cost nothing until data changes, which is the point: the price of the safety net is the data you replaced, not the files you kept.

The detail that trips everyone: a snapshot of the root subvolume does not include the other subvolumes. /home living as its own subvolume means the home snapshots are a separate schedule, or they are silently absent.

Rollback is where I stop improvising. btrfs subvolume set-default <id> / and a reboot beats moving directories around by hand — and doing it once in advance, on purpose, is what makes it boring when it matters.

item.title: Docker to containerd: what changed in the runtime path
item.description:
Docker was never removed from the equation as much as demoted: it already ran on containerd and runC internally. The migration replaced the shim — Kubelet → Docker daemon → containerd — with a direct CRI path, removing daemon layers the node never needed.

The reported effects are the kind ops notices: pod startup latency dropping from tens of seconds to a couple in cited tests, lower Kubelet CPU, and a smaller attack surface since a containerd-only node can’t build and run images locally. Memory usage barely changes; the wins are latency, CPU, and blast radius.

item.title: eBPF: kernel hooks, maps, and tooling
item.description:
eBPF is a small virtual machine inside the kernel. You write a program, the verifier checks it can’t take the machine down, the JIT compiles it, and it attaches to a hook: tracepoints (stable, predefined), kprobes (almost any kernel function), uprobes (user-space functions). Data leaves through maps, because the program stack is 512 bytes and statistics are bigger than that.

The name no longer means Berkeley Packet Filter and the technology isn’t only for clusters — it runs on any Linux box. The on-ramp is bpftrace: one-liners first, BCC or Aya when you need real programs. High-level tooling is the difference between “hard to start” and a tracing session before lunch.

item.title: fuser: processes holding files, mounts, and ports
item.description:
fuser is in the Single UNIX Specification and in nobody’s list of favorite commands, and yet it resolves the two oldest “why is this stuck” questions: the USB drive that won’t unmount, and the port something still holds.

fuser /media/disk lists PIDs; add -v to get user, access type, and command name — enough to discover the forgotten vim in a directory you cd’d into yesterday. -m works on mount points and stays portable across distros. For ports, -n tcp 3000 finds the stale dev server you thought you killed.

item.title: Linux kernel modules: loading, blacklisting, and runtime parameters
item.description:
Modules are how a working kernel stays untouched while gaining drivers and protocols on demand. That design has three practical consequences.

lsmod’s “Used by” column is a dependency graph; ignore it and you’ll learn why rmmod fails where modprobe -r succeeds. modinfo is the map: file location, description, and — the useful part — parameters. And most parameters are adjustable at runtime under /sys/module/<name>/parameters/, which is often the entire fix (connection tracking is the classic example).

item.title: Microservices as technical debt
item.description:
The reason to split a monolith is rarely traffic. High-scale monoliths exist. What doesn’t scale is two hundred developers merging into one deploy: release trains, one bad commit rolling back everyone, rollout time going from hours to days. Microservices solve the people problem by letting a team opt out of the shared release — and that’s the trade.

Debt framing fits: you borrow velocity today against coordination costs tomorrow. The bill shows up as distributed monoliths where every service in the call graph must be up, synchronized deploys for one feature, thousand-RPC requests behind a single page, and alert fatigue when latency pages ten teams at once. Most companies run this way; true loose coupling is hard and expensive.

item.title: Postgres as an all-in-one platform: features and trade-offs
item.description:
The “just use Postgres” talk is seductive because the list is real: JSONB as a document store, tsvector for full-text search, pgvector for embeddings, unlogged tables as a cache, a jobs table with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED as a queue, LISTEN/NOTIFY as pub/sub, pg_cron for scheduling. A .NET app can do all of it through Npgsql. One component to operate, back up, and secure.

My reading is less maximalist than the talk’s. Replacing Redis and a broker with tables is a real simplification for small systems, and a real coupling problem for big ones — every workload now shares one failure domain and one upgrade window. The extensions are production-worthy to varying degrees, and “unorthodox” is a fair description of several.

item.title: Container primitives: namespaces, cgroups, and OverlayFS
item.description: A container is not a box and not a VM. It’s a process that got three kernel features arranged around it: namespaces decide what it can see (its own PIDs, network, mounts — enough to believe it’s PID 1), cgroups decide how much it can use (CPU, memory, PIDs — read live under /sys/fs/cgroup), and a union filesystem stacks image layers with copy-on-write, which is why startup is fast and why the first write to a large file is slow.

item.title: Coding agents in .NET: framework options
item.description:
The framework landscape splits by layer: Semantic Kernel for .NET orchestration (the closest thing to LangChain with types), LlamaIndex and Haystack for retrieval pipelines, AutoGen for multi-agent experiments. Python still owns the build-an-agent ecosystem; .NET teams call it over HTTP when a piece is missing.

The trend worth noting for 2025–2026 is away from magic. Fewer teams adopt a heavyweight framework end to end; more use the OpenAI/Azure SDKs directly, plus a vector store, plus orchestration they wrote themselves and can debug. LangChain-style abstraction reads as overhead once agents are in production and the failure mode is “why did it call that tool.”

item.title: Local LLMs: GGUF, quantization, and Ollama
item.description: Under Ollama is llama.cpp, the C/C++ inference engine, and under that is GGUF: one file bundling weights, tokenizer, and quantization scheme. Quantization is the whole game for local use — a 7B model is ~14 GB at FP16, ~7 GB at Q8, and ~4.5 GB at Q4_K_M. That last row is the only reason any of this runs on a laptop, and Q4_K_M is the default bet for CPU speed versus quality.

item.title: Homelab services: Huginn, Frigate NVR, and streaming
item.description:
The homelab isn’t a rack; it’s a few containers doing jobs nothing else does. The one that earns the most: Huginn as self-hosted IFTTT — watch a product page, diff it, message Telegram when the price drops. Less exciting but more useful than any dashboard I’ve built.

The rest: a media stack, and Frigate for cameras with local object detection. Frigate is the reason I’d argue for a homelab at all — the cloud alternative is a subscription and a privacy decision at once, and neither is reversible once the clips are on someone else’s disk.

item.title: Steam Deck: Gamescope, display, and power settings
item.description:
Borderless windowed is the default that keeps everything working: FSR plays nicer, suspend/resume stays stable, the Steam overlay stays reachable, and the performance difference is negligible. Exclusive fullscreen is for specific stutter cases, not a general setting.

Gaming Mode already runs inside Gamescope, so scaling and FSR are system-wide — set a lower internal resolution and let the compositor upscale. Docked, launch options do the same explicitly (gamescope -f -h 720 -F fsr -- %command%). Games from Heroic should go through Steam shortcuts so they stay inside that compositor instead of fighting it.

item.title: .NET diagnostics: tools and investigation method
item.description:
At scale, a sub-1% bug happens daily, and the method matters more than the profiler: gather trustworthy data, form a hypothesis, verify it — and distrust the model in your head. Two cases keep me honest about that.

Lock contention climbing for weeks traced to TimerQueueTimer.Fire. A reference cycle kept a timer’s TimerHolder reachable from the static timer queue, so the finalizer that exists for exactly this never ran. Fix: IDisposable on anything owning a timer, plus a belt-and-braces finalizer placed outside the cycle.

item.title: Arch Linux suspend/resume loop: causes and fixes
item.description:
Lid closes, machine sleeps, wakes, and fifteen seconds later systemd-logind puts it back to sleep. Repeat until battery is art. The logs look like a single bug, but the loop had three causes, each enough on its own.

Thunderbolt 4 wake sources (TXHC, TDM0) were enabled in /proc/acpi/wakeup; the machine woke on its own, then GNOME’s power daemon saw an idle session and re-suspended it. A oneshot systemd unit now clears those at boot, leaving XHCI enabled so the keyboard still wakes it. Separately, the DDR5 temperature driver (spd5118) failed async resume with -6 on every wake — blacklisted. And a USB receiver was waking the machine too; a udev rule disables that.

item.title: ImageMagick: conversions, batches, and v6/v7 differences
item.description:
Every few years an image tool arrives with a nicer UI, and every few years I’m still typing magick. Converting (JPG→PNG→WebP), resizing, cropping, quality flags: one command each, no project file. magick input.png -quality 85 output.webp still beats opening anything. mogrify for batches, identify when I need to know what a file actually is.

What keeps it alive is that it’s a pipeline citizen: reads stdin, writes stdout, exits with codes, composes with find and xargs. The 400-screenshot problem is one line, not a GUI session.

item.title: MCP servers: catalog, curation, and permissions
item.description:
Model Context Protocol standardizes what every agent framework was already improvising: how a model reaches tools and data. The server catalog covers filesystem, git, databases, documentation lookup, browsers via Playwright, chat, and monitoring. The protocol itself is the least interesting part — it’s plumbing that removed a per-vendor integration tax.

The decision that matters is curation. Each server is a capability with permissions and failure modes; five well-scoped servers beat a marketplace of thirty. For coding workflows, the stack that earns its place is small: filesystem, git, current docs (Context7 exists precisely because training data is stale), and a browser when the task is web-shaped.

item.title: Backups that survive you: restic and B2
item.description:
One restic repository per machine, encrypted with a passphrase that lives somewhere other than the machine. Backups run from a systemd timer, and the retention policy is explicit:

1

restic forget --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 5 --keep-monthly 12 --prune

Backblaze B2 holds the repo because it is cheap and boring, which is the highest praise storage can get.

The part that makes it a backup rather than a hope: a monthly restore drill that pulls three random files to /tmp and diffs them. An untested backup is a rumor.

item.title: WireGuard at home, the boring way
item.description:
One key pair per peer, one config file per peer, wg-quick up — and then it stays up across reboots via the systemd unit, which is the part people reinvent.

The home side allows exactly one CIDR and one port. The other side routes nothing except that CIDR; split tunnel by default, because my laptop belongs to hotels as much as to me.

MTU 1420 belongs in every config on a consumer router, and the first symptom of getting it wrong is the one that sends people back to logs: SSH works, large pushes hang. That note has saved me an afternoon twice.

item.title: A field guide to NuGet central package management
item.description:
Central package management moves every version into one Directory.Packages.props, and suddenly “which version is this solution on” has one answer instead of forty.

The migration order that worked: add the props file, ManagePackageVersionsCentrally, strip versions from every csproj, restore, then fix the one project that legitimately disagrees with a VersionOverride — and write a comment explaining why, because future-you will delete it otherwise.

Transitive pinning is the sharp edge: it can unify versions that were quietly different, so I run the full test suite after the first central restore, not after tidying the props file.

item.title: Delta: the git pager I should have known about
item.description:
The diff is the most-read output in a developer’s day, and it looked like 1998 until I set two lines:

1
2
3
4

[core]
 pager = delta
[interactive]
 diffFilter = delta --color-only

Side-by-side mode for reviewing my own work before pushing, unified for reading a PR, and line numbers so “the third hunk” becomes a coordinate instead of a description.

It changes nothing about git. It changes how much of the diff I actually read, which changes what I catch before anyone else has to.

item.title: AWS SSO for personal accounts
item.description:
A personal AWS account deserves the same credential hygiene as a company one, and Identity Center makes it cheap: one admin user, one permission set, and aws configure sso writing profiles into ~/.aws/config.

After that, the muscle memory is --profile, and the long-lived access keys that used to live in ~/.aws/credentials are deleted. Nothing hangs off root except the billing alarm.

The cost is a browser login every eight hours. That is the feature.

item.title: Hario Switch: the recipe I keep
item.description:
Twenty grams in, 300 out, water at 93. Bloom with 60 grams for forty seconds with the switch closed, pour to 150 by the minute, then open the switch and pour the rest in circles.

The switch is the part that earned its place: a closed steep at the start makes the first pour forgiving of a wobbly kettle, and the drawdown stays even when the grind drifts a click.

item.title: C# collection expressions in real code
item.description:
int[] a = [1, 2, 3] is tidy, but the syntax earns its keep in expressions, not declarations: spread operators turn “new list from those items plus this one” into one line instead of a loop or a AddRange.

1

var targets = [.. defaults, .. overrides, extra];

Two places I still write it out: public APIs where the concrete type is part of the contract, and anywhere the compiler silently picks Span<T> and the benchmark disagrees with the aesthetics.

item.title: Reading notes: A Philosophy of Software Design
item.description:
The book’s durable idea for me is the deep module: an interface narrow enough to hold in your head over an implementation big enough to be worth hiding. Every time I have split a class “for single responsibility” and ended up with three shallow wrappers, this is the counterweight.

The second: complexity is anything that makes a future change harder, and dependencies are the main supplier. That definition turns design arguments into questions with answers — what would this make harder, for whom, when.

item.title: Creating a Maintainable Resume with Markdown and Pandoc
item.description: Keeping a professional resume updated and adaptable for various applications can be a challenging. This post demonstrates how leveraging Markdown for content and Pandoc for conversion simplifies the process, enabling you to maintain a single, clean source file that effortlessly transforms into polished PDF, DOCX, or HTML outputs.

item.title: Down the Rabbit Hole of creating a Home Lab
item.description: Setting up a home lab is an incredible journey that opens up countless learning opportunities in system administration, networking, security, and modern deployment practices. While it might seem daunting at first, the knowledge gained is invaluable for any tech enthusiast or IT professional. In this post, I'll share a practical overview of how I use my home lab, highlighting the real-world projects I've tackled and the key lessons learned along the way. From self-hosting essential services to experimenting with automation, networking, and security, I'll focus on the hands-on experiences that have shaped my understanding of home server management and modern IT practices.

item.title: Server-side rendered SPAs with ASP.NET and no Javascript
item.description: Single-page applications (SPA) provide better user experience by removing full-page loads, giving smooth transitions between pages and performance improvements depending on the scale of the application, but they come at some costs which may not be worth for some application types. The main cost is the added complexity of a SPA framework like Angular or Vue. In this post, I'll show how to use ASP.NET and HTMX to build single-page applications without using JavaScript and SPA frameworks.

item.title: Integration tests with AWS S3 buckets using Localstack and Testcontainers
item.description: As I explained previously in this article, in integration tests, we should mock unmanaged dependencies (dependencies that are external to our system and not controlled by us, like APIs) but test against real managed dependencies (dependencies that are controlled by our system, like databases, queues, etc). This improves the reliability of the integration tests because the communication with these dependencies are a complex part of the system and can break with a package update, a database update or a change in a queue message format. In this post, I'll show how to use Localstack and Testcontainers to emulate an AWS environment for use in integration tests.

item.title: Lessons learned from building a static code analyzer for C#
item.description: Static code analyzers are tools used to analyze software code without executing it. They can examine the code to find code smells, vulnerabilities, potential errors, and code out of a defined standard, for example. They work by parsing the source code and evaluating its syntax (structure of the code) and semantic (meaning of the code). Roslyn, the C# compiler, provides tools for developing Roslyn Analyzers (Static code analyzers for Roslyn), giving access to the syntax and semantic of the code, that can be executed at development and build time, providing feedback in near real-time to the developers. In this post, I'll show a Roslyn Analyzer I built for using Discriminated Unions in C#, requiring to check the union type before access, and talk about some lessons learned while developing it.

item.title: Building a Who's that Pokémon game for Android with .NET MAUI and Blazor Hybrid
item.description: Blazor was initially developed to build interactive web applications using C#, but can now be used in many platforms when used together with .NET MAUI. In this post, I'll show how to use Blazor Hybrid to develop a Who's that Pokémon game for Android.

item.title: How to run scripts on SQL Server container startup
item.description: Unlike MySQL and PostgreSQL, which execute scripts in the /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/ directory after initialization, the SQL Server container image doesn't provide a built-in mechanism for running scripts at startup. In this post, I'll show how to create a custom container image that waits for SQL Server startup and runs a pre-configured script. In addition, I'll show how to use this custom image to run SQL Server in Testcontainers.

item.title: Why my WireMock mocks aren't working?
item.description: WireMock.Net is a great tool to remove external dependencies when writing integration tests, but because it is highly configurable, it can be hard to find why its mocks aren't working. In this post, I'll explain how to troubleshoot problems in its configuration and show some common problems that happen in my day-to-day work.

item.title: .NET and AWS S3 with LocalStack: How to develop with local S3 buckets
item.description: LocalStack is an open-source framework that allows us to emulate the major AWS services locally, making it easier to develop and test cloud applications without incurring the cost and complexity of deploying to a real cloud environment. In this post, I'll show how to configure it to emulate S3 buckets and how to interact with those buckets from a C# application.

item.title: How to use C# 11 features in .NET 6 or older versions (even .NET Framework 2.0)
item.description: At each release, C# adds features that help us make our codes cleaner, more readable and more maintainable. The problem is that, because some features are dependent of runtime implementations, C# versions are generally tied to .NET runtime versions. For example, C# 11 is enabled only in .NET 7 and above. In this post, I'll show how to use C# 11 in older runtime version (even .NET Framework 2.0).

item.title: How to run disposable databases for your tests. Improve your integration tests accuracy with Testcontainers
item.description: Integration tests are essential to ensure that the different components of our system work together as expected and continue to work after changes. In this post, I'll explain how to spin up disposable database containers to use in integration tests.

item.title: Time-out requests in ASP.NET Core with cancellation tokens
item.description: When ASP.NET Core is running in an AWS Lambda and receiving requests through an AWS API Gateway, the application is not notified of an API Gateway time-out and keeps processing the request, completing it eventually. This will leave metrics and logs of a successful request when the client received a time-out error. In this post, I'll show how to solve this problem with cancellation tokens and time-outs.

item.title: Canceling abandoned requests in ASP.NET Core
item.description: When a client makes an HTTP request, the client can abort the request, leaving the server processing if it's not prepared to handle this scenario; wasting its resources that could be used to process other jobs. In this post, I'll show how to use Cancellation Tokens to cancel running requests that were aborted by clients.

item.title: Keep your diagrams updated with continuous delivery
item.description: Changing software diagrams is hard. The simple act of adding a new box may require us to drag all the existing boxes and reorganize the diagram. This is one of the main reasons to why software diagrams are constantly left deprecated after the first stages of the development process. In this post I'll show how defining diagrams as code can help in designing and updating software diagrams, and how to automate the process of updating the documentation with those diagrams.

item.title: Cleaner representation of software architectures with the C4 Model
item.description: Diagrams are a great way to visually communicate something. However, the majority of software architecture diagrams don't really express what they intend to, lacking description of its elements and with lots of implicit notations only understood by who drew the diagram. Also, they try to express more than one vision (high level, infrastructure, flow order, etc) in only one diagram, making it even harder for non technical people or people outside the project to understand. In this post, I'll present the C4 model and how it can produce software architecture diagrams that are inclusive to non-technical people, easier to understand and, consequently, better to document our software systems.

item.title: Analyzing and enforcing .NET code coverage with coverlet
item.description: Automated software tests are a requirement for ensuring we are delivering a product with quality to our users. It helps in finding bugs and requirements not fulfilled at development time, but also decreases the cost of maintenance by making the future changes to our code safer. Besides, the act of writing testable code alone increases the quality of the code we are writing because testable code has to be decoupled. In this last post of this series, I'll show how to analyze and enforce a minimum code coverage in our applications, and how to use integration tests to increase our testing surface.

item.title: Enforcing .NET code style rules at compile time
item.description: Static code analysis is a great tool for spotting some kinds of error in your code, for example, not disposing of objects that implement IDisposable. Also, it helps to enforce and validate if the code written is following a defined standard, for example, using PascalCase for class names and camelCase for parameter names. In this post I'll show how to use Roslyn Analyzers with C# to enforce some standards of code quality and code style on your code, throwing errors at compile time if any rules are not being respected and not allowing the code to be pushed to protected branches of the repository.

item.title: Defining formatting rules in .NET with EditorConfig
item.description: When working with other people and multiple editors/IDEs, it is common to have different editor settings, losing consistency in formatting styles of the code. For example: Using tabs/spaces and different sizes of indentation, making your code harder to read; Using different encoding between files, causing hard to find bugs at runtime (showing invalid characters) and breaking automated tests. In this post I'll show how to maintain a standard for everyone who works in the code, no matter the editor used, and in a next post I'll show how to enforce these (and other) rules on build and in the continuous integration pipeline.

item.title: Integration tests without API dependencies with ASP.NET Core and WireMock.Net
item.description: Although there are many definitions about the scope of an integration test, Martin Fowler defines Narrow integration tests, where the integration with other systems are tested using mocks, and Broad integration tests, where they communicate using real APIs. In this post, I'll explain how to create mocks for HTTP APIs in narrow integration tests using the WireMock.Net library.
